chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Statistical Arbitrage Actually Is

lessons.title: Mean Reversion: The Statistical Idea Stat Arb Is Built On

children.text: Stretch a rubber band and let go, and it snaps back toward its resting length. Push a raft out into a river current, and it keeps drifting downstream, never returning to where it started. Most things that move in markets behave like one of these two objects, and the entire logic of statistical arbitrage rests on being able to tell them apart. A price relationship that behaves like the rubber band, pulled back toward some stable level whenever it stretches too far, is worth building a strategy around. A price relationship that behaves like the raft, drifting wherever the current takes it with no pull back toward anywhere in particular, is not, no matter how tempting the chart looks on a given day.

body.text: Mean reversion is the idea that a variable, after moving away from its typical or average level, tends to drift back toward that level over time, rather than wandering off unpredictably. It is the single statistical property that makes a spread tradeable, and the one Chapter 3 will teach you to test for formally rather than eyeball.

children.text: A mean-reverting series has three ingredients working together: a stable central level it tends to hover around, deviations from that level that are temporary rather than permanent, and something that behaves like a restoring force, pulling the series back whenever it strays too far. None of this means the series cannot move a great deal in the short run. It means that however far it strays, the pull back toward its typical level is, on average, stronger than whatever pushed it away in the first place.
Mean Reversion vs Random Walk: Two Very Different Worlds

columns.label: Mean-Reverting Series
points: Has a stable long-run average it keeps returning to
A large deviation today makes a move back toward the average more likely tomorrow
Variance of the series stays bounded, it does not keep growing the longer you watch it
The kind of behavior a stat arb spread needs in order to be tradeable

columns.label: Random Walk / Trending Series
points: Has no stable level; today's value is the best guess for tomorrow's, plus noise
A large deviation today tells you nothing about tomorrow's direction
Variance keeps growing the longer you watch it, with no ceiling
Most individual stock prices behave close to this on their own

children.text: The difference shows up clearly when you simulate the two side by side, starting from the exact same point.

body.title: Mean-reverting vs trending series, same starting point (illustrative)

body.text: Both series start at exactly 100 and experience similarly sized period-to-period moves. The mean-reverting series keeps being pulled back toward 100 and ends close to where it started. The trending series has no such pull. It drifts further from its starting point the longer you watch it, which is exactly the behavior you do not want in a spread you plan to trade.

children.text: Where You Have Already Seen This: The Nifty PE Ratio

One of the most widely watched mean-reverting series in Indian markets is not a single stock at all, it is the Nifty 50's trailing price-to-earnings ratio. Over long stretches, Nifty's PE has tended to oscillate around a long-run average commonly cited in the high teens to low twenties, spiking well above that range during periods of euphoria and falling well below it during periods of panic, before eventually working its way back. The mechanism pulling it back is straightforward: a PE ratio that has run far ahead of earnings eventually gets reined in, either by prices correcting, by earnings catching up, or some mix of both.

children.text: Reversion Speed: The Half-Life of a Deviation

markDefs.definition: The average time it takes for half of a given deviation from the mean to fade away. A common way to describe how fast, not just whether, a series mean-reverts.

children.text: Knowing that something is mean-reverting is only half the picture. The other half is how fast it reverts. Statisticians and quants describe this with the

, the average time it takes for half of a given deviation from the mean to fade away. A series with a half-life of three trading days pulls back quickly and can, in principle, support a strategy that enters and exits within days or weeks. A series with a half-life of three years is still mean-reverting in a strict statistical sense, but locking up capital in a trade for years to capture a small, slow-moving edge is rarely worth it once you account for what else that capital could be doing.

body.caption: λ (lambda) is the speed of reversion, estimated from historical data. You will compute the inputs needed for this once you build a real regression-based spread in Chapter 2, and formally test whether the reversion is statistically genuine in Chapter 3.
Illustrative half-lives across different mean-reverting phenomena

cells: Nifty futures-cash basis reverting to fair value
Yes, but capital-intensive and dominated by institutional desks
A cointegrated stock pair (e.g. two comparable auto or FMCG names)
Yes. This is the range most retail and prop stat arb strategies target
Sector relative performance (e.g. IT vs Banking)
Difficult. Capital gets tied up a long time relative to the edge captured

body.text: A relationship can be genuinely, statistically mean-reverting and still be a poor trade. If the half-life is measured in years, transaction costs become a rounding error next to the real cost: capital tied up for years chasing a small, uncertain edge instead of being deployed elsewhere. The pairs and baskets built later in this course all target half-lives closer to days and weeks, for exactly this reason.

children.text: Why "It Looks Mean-Reverting on the Chart" Isn't Enough

Stare at almost any six-month stretch of almost any spread and you can usually convince yourself it looks range-bound. That is not the same as the spread being genuinely mean-reverting. A series can wander within a range purely by chance for a while and then break out of it entirely, especially over a short window. Confusing "looks range-bound on this one chart" with "is statistically mean-reverting" is one of the most common mistakes new stat arb traders make, and it is exactly the gap that formal statistical testing exists to close. Chapter 3 introduces stationarity and the tests, the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test and the Engle-Granger method, that separate a spread that is actually mean-reverting from one that only looks that way in hindsight.

body.title: Range-bound, or just lucky?
body.scenario: You pull up six months of daily data for the price ratio of two mid-cap NBFC stocks. It has bounced between 1.8 and 2.1 for the entire period, never breaking out. A friend says, "this is clearly mean-reverting, let's trade it."
body.prompt: What would you want to check before agreeing with him?
body.modelAnswer: Six months is a short window, and a series can stay range-bound by chance over a short stretch without being genuinely mean-reverting. Before trading it, you would want a longer history to see if the range has held up across different market regimes, and ideally a formal statistical test (covered in Chapter 3) rather than relying on how the chart looks over one particular six-month window. You would also want an economic reason the two NBFCs should be linked in the first place, not just that their ratio happened to stay in a band.

body.title: Mean-reverting or random walk?
body.question: A stock's daily price changes are, on average, completely unrelated to whether it rose or fell the day before, and its price has wandered from ₹200 to ₹850 over three years with no sign of returning toward any earlier level. This price series most closely resembles:
options: A series with a very short half-life
A spread that is ready to trade
body.explanation: No stable level to return to, and no relationship between past and future moves, are the hallmarks of a random walk or trending series, not a mean-reverting one. Most individual stock prices behave close to this on their own, which is exactly why stat arb builds spreads out of two related stocks instead of trading one in isolation.

cards.definition: The tendency of a variable to drift back toward a stable, typical level after deviating from it, rather than wandering off unpredictably.
A series whose future changes are unrelated to its past changes, with no stable level to return to and variance that grows the longer you watch it.
The average time it takes for half of a given deviation from the mean to fade away. Shorter half-lives are generally more practically tradeable.
An informal way of describing whatever economic or behavioral mechanism pulls a mean-reverting series back toward its typical level after it strays.

points: Mean reversion means a variable drifts back toward a stable level after deviating from it. A random walk has no such pull and can drift indefinitely.
A mean-reverting series has bounded variance over time; a random walk's variance keeps growing the longer you watch it.
The Nifty PE ratio is a familiar Indian example of mean reversion: it has repeatedly stretched away from its long-run range during euphoria or panic, then reverted.

The half-life of mean reversion tells you how fast a deviation fades. Fast half-lives (days to weeks) are generally tradeable; multi-year half-lives usually are not, once capital efficiency is considered.
A spread that looks range-bound on one chart is not proof that it is genuinely mean-reverting. Chapter 3 introduces the formal statistical tests that make that distinction properly.
